objectives.wording: Mark the named horizontal and vertical reference lines, linea alba and linea semilunaris on a model. Use them to locate the nine regions and four quadrants.
On a model mark the abdominal regions and planes, both inguinal rings, McBurney point, renal angle and Murphy point.
On a torso mark the stomach, liver, gallbladder fundus, spleen, duodenum, pancreas, ileocaecal junction, kidneys and mesenteric root.
On a model identify fascial planes and trace the segmental nerves and major vessels through the wall.
Draw the sheath above and below the arcuate line and locate its muscular and neurovascular contents.
Show the attachments of the anterolateral abdominal muscles and trace their aponeuroses to the midline.
Demonstrate the rings, walls, extent and contents on a model and locate the boundaries of the inguinal triangle.
Trace direct and indirect hernia routes relative to the deep ring and inferior epigastric vessels.
Locate congenital and acquired diaphragmatic hernias and explain how their positions shape presentation.
Compare representative incisions by exposure, layers crossed and potential injury to nerves or vessels.
Draw the fascial layers in section and identify their vertebral, rib and pelvic attachments and extent.
Identify major intrinsic back muscle groups on a specimen or model and relate each group's innervation to its actions.
Trace its roots and branches on a model and use their courses to predict findings after a representative root or branch lesion.
Side and orient a specimen, identify coverings and internal structures, and trace descent and vascular, neural and lymphatic routes. Use those routes to explain a clinical correlation.
Locate the head, body and tail and trace sperm passage from the efferent ductules to the ductus deferens.
Describe the parts, components, blood supply and lymphatic drainage of the penis.
Trace testicular venous drainage on both sides and relate the asymmetry to the typical distribution of varicocele.
Locate the foreskin, preputial opening and frenulum and explain how their relationships account for phimosis and inform circumcision.
Trace the peritoneum in horizontal and sagittal sections, show the boundaries and recesses of both sacs and locate their communication.
Identify principal folds and dependent pouches on a model and explain what each connects or contains.
Identify the subphrenic compartments and explain how ligament boundaries and paracolic pathways influence abscess location.
Map routes by which free fluid and inflammation can spread through the peritoneal cavity.

Use a specimen or model to orient each major abdominal viscus. Identify external and internal landmarks and peritoneal relations, then trace vascular, neural and lymphatic pathways and explain a clinical correlation for each.

Use separate cases to explain splenic notches, accessory spleens and Kehr sign, vagotomy, liver biopsy landmarks, biliary obstruction and referred pain, periumbilical and loin-to-groin pain, and gastric cancer lymphatic spread.
On a model distinguish the classical triangle from the modern hepatocystic triangle and locate the cystic artery and nearby ducts.
Describe and identify the formation, course, relations and tributaries of the portal vein, inferior vena cava and renal veins.
Describe the sites of portosystemic anastomoses, their applied anatomy and anatomical correlations.
Explain how oesophageal varices can cause haematemesis and how paraumbilical collateral flow produces caput medusae.
On a model trace the abdominal aorta and the coeliac, superior mesenteric, inferior mesenteric and common iliac arteries, identifying their origins, relations and major branches.
Map the major prevertebral plexuses and trace autonomic fibres to representative abdominal targets.
On a model show diaphragmatic attachments and major openings, trace innervation and demonstrate the effect of contraction on thoracic volume.
Orient male and female pelvic models and identify each major viscus and its relations. Trace arterial, neural and lymphatic routes and explain representative clinical correlations.
Use pelvic diagrams to explain suprapubic bladder access, prostatic obstruction, uterine retroversion and prolapse, haemorrhoids and anal fistula, vasectomy, tubal pregnancy and tubal ligation.
Identify the levator ani subdivisions and coccygeus and show their attachments, openings and support functions.
Trace its course and relations on a model and distinguish the anterior and posterior divisions by their major branches and territories.
Map the principal branches to their root contributions and pelvic, perineal or lower-limb targets.
Trace the sacral micturition reflex and explain how loss of descending control can permit reflex emptying after spinal shock resolves.
Map traditional lobes and modern zones and identify the usual regions of benign enlargement and carcinoma.
On diagrams of vaginal and rectal examination, identify normally accessible structures and explain how anatomy determines palpability.
Use male and female models to delimit superficial and deep perineal spaces and identify their contents.
Locate the perineal body on a model, identify major muscular attachments and explain its support role.
Demonstrate attachments and structures traversing the membrane in male and female models.
Show its boundaries, fat, pudendal canal and communicating spaces on a model and explain routes of abscess spread.
Use sectional diagrams to explain perineal tears, episiotomy anatomy, perianal abscess and the pain and location of anal fissures.
Sketch primary and secondary curvatures and relate their development to posture.
On a model classify intervertebral, sacroiliac and pubic joints, locate surfaces and ligaments, and demonstrate their permitted motion.
Use diagrams to distinguish scoliosis, exaggerated lordosis, disc prolapse, spondylolisthesis and spina bifida by the structures involved.
On a sagittal diagram select a lumbar interspace below the usual adult conus, indicate the needle trajectory and sequence the layers to the subarachnoid space.
Orient axial sections at T8, T10 and L1 and identify the organs, vessels and vertebral landmarks that distinguish the levels.
Orient male and female midsagittal images and identify organ relationships, peritoneal reflections and the pelvic floor.
Identify histological slides of the digestive tract, its glands and the adrenal gland.
Identify the epithelial transition at the gastro-oesophageal junction.

Identify kidney, ureter, bladder, testis, epididymis, vas deferens, prostate, penis, ovary, uterus, uterine tube, cervix, placenta and umbilical cord slides. Justify each identification with a structural feature.
Identify the luteal cell populations of the corpus luteum.
Diagram lateral embryonic folding and ventral body wall closure, marking the umbilical ring.
Map the embryonic contributions to the diaphragm and explain how an abnormal contribution or fusion can produce a congenital defect.
Trace foregut, midgut and hindgut derivatives and use staged diagrams to explain representative anomalies of each region.
Trace formation of the kidneys and collecting system, renal ascent and development of the bladder and urethra.
Trace gonadal differentiation, duct development and formation of the external genitalia in male and female development.
Orient representative lumbar and pelvic bones, identify major landmarks and articulations, and demonstrate representative muscle attachments.
Orient an articulated pelvis and demonstrate the boundaries of the inlet, cavity and outlet.
Identify the pelvic brim, distinguish the true and false pelvis and compare sex-associated features using multiple landmarks.
Identify sacralization, lumbarization, pelvic shape variants and coccygeal landmarks on models or images and explain their clinical relevance.
Compare how plain and contrast radiography, CT, MRI, PET and digital subtraction angiography generate anatomical or functional information.
Match ERCP, CT, MRI and arteriography to representative diagnostic questions and explain the structures each can delineate.
Orient a plain abdominal film and identify expected skeletal landmarks, gas patterns and soft-tissue outlines.
Identify barium swallow, meal and enema, cholecystography, intravenous pyelography and hysterosalpingography images using the opacified structures and route.
Identify dura, arachnoid and pia on a model and demonstrate their extent and major cranial and spinal specializations.
Trace CSF from production through the ventricles and subarachnoid space to absorption and predict the consequences of obstruction at different sites.
